title: Research Trends in Respiratory Syncytial Virus: A Ten-Year Bibliometric Analysis and the Translational Evolution of Dual Strategies for Prevention
content: Background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) has always been a leading cause of acute lower respiratory infections in vulnerable age groups since its identification in 1956. Despite more than half a century of attempts, the effective preventive strategies only arrived recently with the approval of the prefusion F protein–based vaccines and the long-acting monoclonal antibodies. A full understanding of how RSV research has changed with the prefusion F protein–based vaccines and the acting monoclonal antibodies helps us see the road of RSV prevention and helps us guide the future prevention steps. Methods: We conducted an analysis of RSV related publications, in the Web of Science Core Collection from 2014 to 2025. The analysis combined citation analysis, collaboration networks, keyword evolution and co citation mapping. In parallel, trials of the RSV monoclonal antibodies and the vaccines that are listed on ClinicalTrials.gov were examined, time span focusing on the studies that started or finished after the milestones. The combined approach linked the research trends to the progress, in the RSV prevention. Results: There were 2,670 publications that were part of the study and what we found out is that people are doing more research on RSV especially after 2019. The United States and China emerged as the most influential contributors, supported by dense international collaboration networks. Keyword and co-citation analyses showed a shift, from virology and disease burden studies to prevention-focused themes. Prevention-focused themes include prefusion F antigen design, monoclonal antibodies, vaccination and hospitalization outcomes. Clinical trial analysis showed that long-acting monoclonal antibodies(especially nirsevimab) have led infant RSV prophylaxis since their development, while recombinant prefusion F protein vaccines make up the majority of vaccine trials, sponsored primarily by major pharmaceutical developers. mRNA, live-attenuated viral vector, and virus-like particle platforms, although not widely used, remain strategically important for generating new approaches. Conclusions: RSV prevention has entered a novel phase which characterized by the convergence of long-acting monoclonal antibodies for infants and effective vaccines for older adults and pregnant women. The integration of bibliometric trends with clinical trial landscapes highlights a transition from exploratory research to implementation-oriented prevention strategies. Future efforts must pay attention to low- and middle-income countries where RSV burden stays highest.
